title: Virginia’s Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel
description:
Imagine driving across open ocean for miles — and then, without warning, the road disappears beneath the water.
This is extraordinary Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel, one of the most remarkable transport engineering achievements in the United States.
Stretching 17.6 miles across the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay, this unique structure links the Norfolk–Hampton Roads region with Cape Charles on the Delmarva Peninsula, creating a direct road where travellers once relied entirely on ferries.
Construction began in 1958, and when the crossing opened in 1964, it transformed travel across one of America’s widest estuaries. The ferry system it replaced had long struggled with weather delays and rising demand, making a permanent link increasingly necessary.
Yet engineers faced a major challenge. The Chesapeake Bay is a vital maritime corridor, serving commercial shipping and one of the world’s largest naval bases in nearby Naval Station Norfolk. A continuous bridge could obstruct large vessels navigating the main channels.
Their solution was ingenious: a bridge–tunnel system combining miles of low-level trestle bridges, high-level spans, artificial islands, and underwater tunnels.
For most of the journey, drivers travel across long bridges that skim just above the water, supported by thousands of concrete pilings. But at two key points — beneath the Thimble Shoal Channel and the Chesapeake Channel — the roadway suddenly dives underground.
Here, the bridge connects to two underwater tunnels, each entered through large man-made islands built from rock and sand in the middle of the bay. These islands act as portals where the highway descends beneath the shipping lanes.
The tunnels themselves were constructed using enormous prefabricated concrete sections, carefully floated into position, lowered into dredged trenches on the seabed, and joined together underwater before being sealed and covered.
This design allows the largest cargo ships and naval vessels to pass safely overhead while motorists travel quietly beneath the bay.
Today, millions of vehicles cross the structure each year, making it a vital transport link that supports regional commerce, tourism, and daily travel across the Delmarva Peninsula.
More than sixty years after opening, the Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel remains a striking example of engineering ingenuity — a place where drivers experience the rare sensation of travelling from open bridge to underwater tunnel and back again, all within a single remarkable journey.
